description.narrative: The Fair, Green and Global Alliance (FGG) aims to increase the power and decision-making influence of organised, mobilised and informed civil society, especially women, to advance fair and green trade and value chains. FGG believes that poverty, inequality and exclusion are caused by power asymmetries. We see the unprecedented power of capital over people and planet as the primary obstacle impeding realisation of fair and green trade and value chains. The FGG programme focuses on recalibrating power within the global architecture of trade and value chains by amplifying the voices of targeted rights-holders – small producers and traders, workers, fishers, rural and Indigenous peoples, religious and ethnic minorities, and migrants, especially the women and youth among them – who are practising, claiming or defending human rights and fair and green economic practices, and/or whose rights are being ignored, threatened or violated by corporations and/or governments. We aim to transform social relations so that these rights-holders’ voices are heard and heeded. FGG’s eight members (ActionAid, Both ENDS, Clean Clothes Campaign, IT for Change, Milieudefensie/Friends of the Earth International/Friends of the Earth Europe, Samdhana Institute, SOMO and the Transnational Institute) cooperate with some 1000+ partners and allies in our many worldwide networks to strengthen collective capacities to advance a common vision of fair and green trade and value chains.

comment.narrative: 1 In 2021, the Governor of Bengkulu in Indonesia issued recommendations for resolving land use rights conflicts. This is the result of farmers’ lobbying, and the recommendation is to establish a GTRA to resolve land conflicts in the district, with the GTRA mandated to resolve the PT land use rights conflict immediately. Samdhana supported the farmer union’s work through grants. 2 In 2021, at least four key actors: Municipal local government unit, barangay (village) local government unit in Misamis Oriental, NCIP offices, and Provincial & Municipal IPMRs, convened and co-organized a dialogue between the Tribal Council and private land sellers and/or buyers to resolve the arising land conflicts. They organized this upon the request of the Tribal Council, and in recognition that the tribe has ownership of the land and has the right to regulate the entry of businesses that intend to operate within the domain. Concrete steps were addressed for each specific case represented by the private individuals who attended the dialogue. The presence of the Local Government Units (LGU) are crucial as most non-IPs defer to the LGU authorities, while the presence of the NCIP, as the main mediating body is also vital. This dialogue is a result of the tribe’s continuous engagement with these agencies for their rights to be recognised as enshrined in the IPRA. Samdhana supported the community leaders’ gatherings and mobilisations. 3 In 2021, the Head of Jayapura Regency, Papua Province in Indonesia publicly called for the protection and development of Jayapura and Yotoro Hill. This is a result of his participation in the Menoken di Tabi, a community gathering, and knowledge exchange facilitated by Samdhana in coordination with other local organisations. The GTMA had a MOU or joint commitment in GTRA for the first time in Papua Province; that will raised both parties determination to pursue a recognition and protection of their territoty.

On Gender Equality, Disability, and Social Inclusion (GEDSI): ●Samdhana formulated a Gender Equality, Disability, and Social Inclusion (GEDSI) Assessment Framework and Methodology that can be used by partner organisations and further localised according to the context of the community or organisation. The GEDSI Assessment Framework was formulated as part of the Institutional GEDSI Audit that Samdhana underwent in 2022. It aimed to assess, analyse, and provide recommendations on the integration and institutionalization of gender mainstreaming into Samdhana’s staffing, policies, programs, projects and services, structures, budget and processes. It provided an opportunity to conduct institutional self – evaluation to determine which GEDSI measures have been implemented within the organization and how these are implemented. The gaps and possible courses of action to improve GEDSI mainstreaming efforts were also identified. The framework focused on five key component areas: Vision, Mission, Goals and Objectives (VMGO), values and principles, HRM, Programming, budgeting, project planning and implementation, research, monitoring, evaluation and learning, and communications and knowledge management. The framework utilised the GEDSI mainstreaming as a continuum in five stages: blind, aware, sensitive, responsive, and transformative. The GEDSI audit result indicated that Samdhana is a highly sensitive organisation that is moving towards responsiveness in its efforts to mainstream GEDSI. It scores highly responsive in its VMGOs, values and principles, programming, budgeting, project planning and implementation, as well as policies and strategies on Human Resource Management, training and development. It also scores highly sensitive in communications and knowledge management, research and MEL (Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning). The GEDSI Audit was also conducted with two other partner organisations – one working on climate science and the other one on legal work. ● A GEDSI mainstreaming action team was formed to lead in the formulation of the institutional Gender Action Plan. This follows the recommendations of the GEDSI audit for Samdhana that was completed in 2022.●In Indonesia, a trainers’ training was held with a focus on the GEDSI module content and structure (https://samdhana.org/publication/analytical-framework-living-space-and-livelihood-gender-equality-and-social-inclusion). Staff in the Philippines-Mekong operations had an orientation on the Gender Equity and Social Inclusion (GESI) framework to further mainstream it across the programs, especially in the context of tenure rights. During the sessions, Staff realized that we have been putting less emphasis on probing the gender situation at the community level. One example is that we do not actively disaggregate statistics, like how many women actually control the land or resources within their collective ancestral domain. One resolution was for the team to prepare better probing questions to surface the gender situation or specific needs of peoples with different abilities. Staff have been practicing basic gender sensitivity, and we improved on those practices. One is ensuring that there is women-to-women facilitation of community discussions and planning activities. We have observed and believe that community women are more free to voice out their concerns when there are no men present. Thus, several female staff are usually designated to handle these sessions. the extent to and ways in which FGG involves local groups in the design and implementation of the FGG programme

comment.narrative: Samdhana aligns its programs according to the identified needs and priorities of the community - from project design to implementation and planning for sustainability, Samdhana accompanies partner IPLCs to ensure that Samdhana’s own goals are aligned with those of its partnersSamdhana aims to enhance and improve the representation of IPLCs in the mobilisation, consultation and involvement that will enable them to represent and promote their efforts and interest in order to bring changes necessary for them to access and assert their rights that will respond to their needs as well as adapting to changing realities in the communities. Samdhana is also flexible in responding to needs of its partners by adapting to changing realities in the communities - these changing needs often signal a need for Samdhana to continue reflecting on its interventions and find more appropriate ways of working with communities given the changing context.

Organisational strengthening of Indigenous Peoples Organisations (IPOs). The FGG programme takes on a mutual capacity development approach in supporting IPOs in terms of strengthening their organisational capacities and governance mechanisms towards tenure rights assertion, promoting agroecology, and asserting for inclusion and participation in government-mandated processes. We do this by first assessing the current needs and capacities of the communities that we work with. We then help them become organised into IPOs with clear organisational structures, and guide them in developing the necessary elements to become their own independent organisations, such as organisational vision and mission, and five-year strategic plans. The strategic plans then serve as a guide for the IPOs with concrete steps towards achieving the goals they have identified for themselves. Aside from a broad, community-based IPO, the women and youth are also guided in establishing their own organisations. This is done to complement the work that is done by the broader IPO, and also for them to be able to pursue their own development needs. Some of these plans are then supported by a small grant, or they are linked up with other service providers who can assist in realising those plans. The hope is that in the long-term, they will be able to manage their own organisations even without support from the FGG programme.Bridging local partners with more CSO partners and networks. This approach aims to bring in more partners and networks working within the same community or thematic areas. This is so that in the long-term, more organisations would be pooling in their support to communities or to specific themes of work, with whom our local partners can align with even after the FGG programme.We still maintain responsive grantsmaking, wherein community initiated/ led and community managed projects are based on community’s plans and proposals. Where possible, Samdhana conducts consultation and facilitation to partners to clarify their proposals and to help them make their projects more realistic and achievable based on the limited funding and duration. Grantee-Partners are given basic skills training to support them to implement their projects, and manage it, especially for financial reporting.

Through the FGG support, we started to widen our reach in the Lower Mekong region, in particular by reaching out to new local CSO partners in Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar and Laos. FGG support was provided through small grantsmaking to these partners, and as such, all projects have been planned and determined by the Partner themselves. We consult with proponents and facilitate that proposals will be improved so that their ideas will be expressed in a clearer manner on the paper proposal. Design of capacity building activities are usually based on needs expressed by community partners, such as the need for crafting their strategic plan or providing a financial literacy training. We hold feedback sessions with community partners and leaders to assess project activities that had been conducted. Communication lines to Samdhana staff are open and this increases the access of community partners to Samdhana where there is open and timely exchange of information that also help us to make informed decisions in relation to the implementation. For the Regional Youth Menoken, we created the youth working groups and allowed each team to design their own program, with minimum guidance from Samdhana; thus the youth were the ones who identified the topics that were shared and discussed.

comment.narrative: Learning was a continuous process internally and externally throughout the year. Internally, Samdhana was able to hold sessions with all Program teams to learn how our work aligns with the FGG Theory of Change, and how the language of trade and value chains translate to or link with Samdhana’s areas of work. We reflected on how Samdhana is supporting Partners, and how Partners lobby and advocate. The orientations provided by the Coordination Team assisted us in determining the outcomes of our support and groundwork. Through these discussions and reflections on our roles and those of our Partners, we, particularly the Philippines team, were able to recognize that government agencies play an important role in the work. Learning sessions and one-on-one online meetings with new partners, especially those from Cambodia and Myanmar, deepened staff members' understanding of context and analysis on key issues such as tenure and resource governance. Part of the internal learning is equipping the staff through a four-part workshop on Mental Health and Psycho-social Support (MHPSS) was designed to address internal staff needs following a year-long personal and professional struggle with the COVID-19 pandemic. This was done in recognition of the fact that, while Samdhana was able to work exceptionally well during the pandemic, staff were also vulnerable to the mental stress and anxiety that the pandemic generally caused. Externally, Samdhana staff and Partners continue a dynamic exchange of lessons and insights in our engagement with them. “Menoken” was an avenue for building interpersonal relationships beyond work or project-related concerns; it fostered exchange of personal stories especially those that motivate people to protect the environment, stand up for their rights and promote their cultures. It provided experiential learning through exchange of products, local culinary arts and crafts. The several sessions on strategic planning or visioning and problem analysis/ assessment with community partners were also avenues to learn of their context and history, their assessment and tactics to address their problems and what they aspire for. With indigenous partners, staff are continuously learning and re-calibrating our use of terms to adopt the local language, and encourage the community to put forth their own model of governance, and not limit it to only what is common today in structures of people organizations or State government. We were also challenged to learn how to maximize communications, especially for IPLC youth who are internet- and gadget-savvy and we continue to explore the online platforms that will be useful for us.

On Advancing Gender Equality: A conversation on Contextualising Gender Equality, Disability and Social Inclusion (GEDSI) in Indigenous Peoples in their respective communitiesIn 2023, Samdhana initiated its efforts on Gender Equality, Disability, and Social Inclusion (GEDSI) by conducting an organisational GEDSI audit along with other CSO partners in the Philippines, which led to the development of the Organisational Gender Action Plans (OGAP) and the establishment of a GEDSI policy within the organisation. However, in 2024, there was a need to revisit GEDSI through the lens of the community, particularly focusing on Indigenous communities. This approach aims to address prevalent gender issues within the community context, tackling deeply entrenched societal norms and structural inequalities that impede the full participation and empowerment of women. By fostering open and respectful dialogue, this initiative will also connect to traditional gender roles while advocating for equal opportunities, and inclusive decision-making processes.This represents a significant step toward promoting GEDSI as a rights-based development strategy among IPLCs. Specifically, it aims to encourage IPLC partners, especially those within Indigenous Political Structures, to ensure that women, men, and individuals of all genders are actively involved in a more gender-sensitive and responsive decision-making process. During this conversation, participants explored various concepts related to GEDSI, including its legal framework, policy mandates, approaches to gender and social inclusion, and the importance of GEDSI mainstreaming—especially in the context of IPLCs. The contextualising resulted into a community action plan drafted to facilitate the transfer of GEDSI knowledge within the community. The GEDSI module was also translated into the local language as part of the contextualisation.

Regional Forum173 participants from eight countries, along with other civil society and non government organisations participated in the 2nd Southeast Regional Forum on Indigenous Peoples’ Rights and Climate Change in the Digital Era last August 9 - 11, 2025. The forum opened with the joint celebration of Hari Internasional Masyarakat Adat Sedunia (HIMAS), or the International Day of the World’s Indigenous People organised and convened by: AMAN, Asia Indigenous Peoples Pact (AIPP), IT for Change, Adaptation Research Alliance – Stockholm Environment Institute, Tifa Foundation, and Samdhana Institute.The Regional Forum includes topics on: Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Practices (IKSPs), Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), Non-Economic Loss and Damage (NELD), and Digitalization and AI: Rights, Resilience and Justice for Indigenous Peoples in a Changing Climate. This has resulted to a Bogor Call of Action that includes recommendations and appeals of Indigenous Peoples to take effective action on core issues they continue to struggle with in asserting their rights and address newer challenges arising from digitalization and artificial intelligenceSoutheast Asia Regional Summit on Food Sovereignty and Climate ResilienceAgroecology work in the last four years have resulted in regional learning and policy lobbying. Samdhana, in partnership with MASIPAG Mindanao, Lem Bulul Farmers Association - a T’boli women led organic farming association, and the Lake Sebu Indigenous Women Weavers Association Inc. (LASIWWAI) organised the Southeast Asia Regional Summit on Food Sovereignty and Climate Resilience in September 2025. The summit successfully consolidated the voices of 81 Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs) from eight countries across Southeast Asia in a “Call to Action” to improve government services and policies, as well as actions of IPLCs themselves and support for them to strengthen food sovereignty and climate resilience for all. This call of action urges policymakers, academia, consumers, civil society, and IPLCs to take concrete steps toward a more just, sustainable, and resilient food future. Youth and Women SummitFor the last five years, Samdhana continued co-creating spaces for women and youth. In April 2025, a landscape youth wide learning exchange was facilitated, this youth summit brought together nine youth organisations , to share their conservation and restoration initiatives and continue ushering a broader community for youth led movement for environmental protection. These youth organisations have been involved in earlier youth camps, such as the Menoken in 2021 and 2022. Another summit was organised for Indigenous women in October 2025. The conversations during the Northern Mindanao-wide summit affirmed the close links between gender, climate change, food security, and agriculture. The IP women participants shared that there is a distinct and often under-recognised role of women in climate change mitigation and adaptation.

There were nine policy recommendations included in the task force’s notes and these are: (1) Financing for short term food and nutrition insecurity, (2) Support food systems transformation toward affordability of healthy diets for all, (3) Investing on resilient food systems and nature positive agricultural production that adapts to climate change and external shocks, (4) Repurposing agricultural subsidies and supports to directly benefit of sustainable practices, (5) Reducing food loss and waste, (6) Investing on smallholders, small-scale producers and family farming, (7) Enhancing food production on the basis of sustainable agriculture practices, (8) Enhancing diversification of food production, supply and inclusive global value chains and (9)Support research and innovation on sustainable food systems. They organised three international symposia and two local talks with topics ranging from food systems transformation and digitalisation in the agriculture sector, to food waste and agri-tech start-ups. 12.In 2022, one CSO partner in the Philippines (1) used its strengthened knowledge to work on the promotion of agroecology in Northern Mindanao landscape and are part of a network that is working closely with the Department of Agriculture in terms of farmer to farmer learning, seed sharing, and development of a Participatory Guarantee System. 13.In 2022, one IP partner in the Philippines (1) through its indigenous lawyer vying for the post of Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representative (IMPR) at the province of Bukidnon, crafted an agenda, as a result of consultations with indigenous leaders. With the consulted agenda, the indigenous lawyer prevailed in the selection process traditionally done by indigenous leaders from all the ancestral domains within the province. This is significant because selection processes in the past had always been influenced by political interests rather than of genuine IP voices. The IP agenda is a reflection of the needs and aspirations of Indigenous Peoples that he, as IPMR, would be lobbying for at the Province. The FGG programme supported the IPMR in organising the agenda formulation workshop and by providing funds to consolidate community leaders. 14.In 2022, one CSO partner in the Philippines (1) garnered media and social media attention for their advocacy on people’s participation in the implementation of a plan to end hunger and poverty among farmer families. 27 farmers and fisherfolks from eight associations and cooperatives, from different regions, undertook a 4,000 km caravan and 400 km march from Sumilao, Bukidnon to Makati City in 41 days, dubbed as “Lakad ng mga Pamilyang Magsasaka Laban sa Gutom at Kahirapan” (or March of family farmers Against Hunger and Poverty). The marching family farmers were able to mobilise six key national coalitions and hundreds of CSOs who organised grand welcome rallies to greet their arrival in their respective town or city centres, join them in the march, and hear them speak and tell their stories. Their overall call was for the effective and efficient implementation of the Philippine Action Plan for Family Farming (PAP4FF), a plan to end hunger and poverty among family farmers by 2028. These events drew great mainstream and social media attention in particular. This is important because the plan needs to be disseminated to the greater public, especially family farmers, so they are able to own it and participate more meaningfully in its implementation. FGG supported this campaign through its small grant.15.In 2022, one CSO partner in the Philippines (1) used its strengthened knowledge to submit a manifesto for environmental conservation and sustainable use of resources to one of the presidential candidates in time for the Philippine presidential elections. This, accompanied by rebuilding the regional sub-formations of its organisation, is important because consolidating the CSO leaders is key to effectively pushing their environmental agenda among political candidates, not only nationally, but also locally in the Western Mindanao landscape of the Philippines. FGG supported this through a small grant and capacity development on project and financial management to assist the alliance in more effectively managing the trainings and other related interventions on its own.16.In 2022, three CBO partners (3) and one NGO partner (1) in the Philippines of returned migrant workers from different communities and tribal organisations advocate for the inclusion of their issues in the local government agenda. They exchanged ideas and shared ideas on pre-election, socio-cultural, and environmental issues and how the political agenda of migrant workers and families should be advanced in relation to these issues. They have crafted a six-month organisational plan that includes organisational accreditation, accessing government agencies’ programs and services, and engaging local leaders in their policy advocacy. The knowledge gained by members of one CBO on the importance of a help desk for migrant workers contributed to their decision to include such an agenda for local policy advocacy in their municipality in Maguindanao, Philippines. FGG’s contribution was through a small grant to a partner NGO, who facilitated the CBO discussions.17.In 2022, one IP youth partner in the Philippines (1) strengthened its organisational structure and developed the capacities of its council officers and members to educate and capacitate more youth on customary laws, leadership and in “sulagad” or traditional farming. This IP youth partner is a member of the Technical Working group in the Youth Noken. As a result of strengthening their organisational structure, the youth partner conducted a campaign and community organising to promote indigenous rights and “sulagad” within their communities. They were able to involve 85 youth advocates in various communities who are doing information, education and communication campaigns and are lending their voices for environmental and human rights issues through social media platforms. They have closely worked with their Indigenous Political Structure, which have already included the youth agenda in the overall ancestral domain priorities. 18.In 2022, two CSO partners in the Philippines (2) increased the capacities of Indigenous Peoples and support networks to engage in democratic spaces and post-election. The State of Indigenous Peoples Address (SIPA) was once again held in 2022 to take stock of the Indigenous Peoples’ situation, especially under the new administration. This was spearheaded by the two organisations as part of their community strengthening and policy development work. Taking off from issues of disinformation as a grave threat to Philippine democracy, the SIPA became a venue for indigenous groups from 12 provinces across the country to take initial scrutiny of the new administrations’ policies and their impacts on natural resources and Indigenous Peoples rights. An advocacy document was then produced signifying the Indigenous Peoples declaration of action and proposed strategies to pursue the IP agenda identified in the previous year’s SIPA. This is important because this is to be the basis for initial policy studies and shall also inform other advocacy campaign tracks of the spearheading organisations. FGG co facilitated this initiative and provided small grants to the organising NGOs. 19.In 2022, one IP partner in the Philippines (1) , who requested a Certificate on Ancestral Domain Title (CADT) to the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) was put on hold because of the newly installed Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARM) who issued a resolution no. 38 for the cease and desist order of the CADT issuance of the IP partner. As a result of this cease and desist order, members of the community were under siege, being victims of land grabbing and displacement, which have resulted in the horrific murder of one of the Indigenous leaders . With these continuous struggles, the IP partner increased awareness of their rights as Indigenous Peoples through an information, education, and communication campaign. The IP partner widened the awareness of their rights, inform government leaders about their rights especially advancing IP rights.

Throughout 2023, we will provide support to 14 IPLC and CSO partners that, based on their enhanced capacities, are actively engaged in territory claims, land issues, and IPLC advocacy campaigns in the Philippines, Indonesia, Cambodia, Myanmar, Laos, and Thailand. These include Indigenous Peoples lobbying towards public policy to gain government recognition by supporting IP Territory claims through mapping, networking, and expanding engagement with government agencies and the relevant task force created for tenure security, to increase partnerships that will provide technical services and support territory claims.The 14 IPLCs and CSOs� lobby work will focus on community mapping, ethnographic data base and policy work to get local government recognition.
